First cut at making `deno compile` ship a bundled entrypoint instead of  
embedding the entire `node_modules/` tree verbatim. Motivated by a  
real-world report comparing `deno compile` against `bun build --compile`  
on a 2700-module CLI, where Deno's binary was ~3x bigger almost entirely  
because of the raw npm payload. The flag is gated behind a "this is  
experimental" warning since several real cases aren't handled yet.

When `--bundle` is set, the entrypoint is run through the existing  
esbuild-based bundler (ESM, platform=Deno, packages=Bundle,  
tree-shaking on) and the bundle is written to a temp `.mjs` next to the  
source. The standalone binary writer then sees a single self-contained  
file in the graph, so the existing managed-npm path naturally skips the  
VFS fill (no `Module::Npm` entries left after tree-shaking). The BYONM  
path, which fills the VFS unconditionally, is gated on the new flag.  
The existing `replace_require_shim` rewrite is reused so esbuild's  
"Dynamic require not supported" stub becomes a real  
`createRequire(import.meta.url)` call against `node:module`, so dynamic  
`require()` of `node:` builtins keeps working in denort.

Known limitations for this PR (intentional, to keep it reviewable):  
native `.node` addons, worker entrypoints, and any module that does  
dynamic `require(path.join(__dirname, ...))` aren't traced and will  
break. CJS npm packages are also currently externalized by esbuild as a  
runtime `require()` against `node_modules`, which `--bundle` strips, so  
those break too; this is locked in by an expected-failure spec  
(`compile/bundle/npm_cjs_unsupported`) that should be removed once CJS  
packages are inlined into the bundle. The warning calls out the  
experimental status.

First-cut feature looks promising in shape — esbuild ESM bundle, the existing `replace_require_shim` + `force_node_cjs_interop` post-processing reused via `maybe_process_contents`, and the managed/byonm VFS fill skipped under `--bundle`. A few things I'd want addressed before this lands.

### Cleanup regression (real, narrow)

The previous code constructed the framework-entrypoint cleanup guard immediately, before any further work:

```rust
let _cleanup = CleanupGuard(_framework_entrypoint_file);
```

The new code defers guard construction until after the bundle step:

```rust
let mut cleanup_paths: Vec<PathBuf> = Vec::new();
if let Some(path) = _framework_entrypoint_file { cleanup_paths.push(path); }
// ...
if compile_flags.bundle {
  let bundle_path = run_bundle_for_compile(&flags, &compile_flags).await?; // <-- ?
  cleanup_paths.push(bundle_path);
  ...
}
let _cleanup = CleanupGuard(cleanup_paths);
```

If `run_bundle_for_compile` returns an error, the function unwinds via `?` before `_cleanup` is created, so the framework entrypoint isn't deleted. Narrow (requires framework auto-detection + `--bundle` + bundle failure) but it's a regression from the prior ordering. Easiest fix: construct the guard before the bundle call and push the bundle path into a shared `Rc<RefCell<Vec<PathBuf>>>`, or use two guards.

### Title `feat(unstable)` vs. implementation

The flag is plain `--bundle` with a runtime stderr warning, not behind `--unstable-*` or a config gate. Other experimental Deno features (KV, etc.) gate behind unstable flags so users opt in explicitly. Either gate this the same way and keep the `feat(unstable)` title, or rename the PR to `feat(compile)` if the warning-only approach is the deliberate choice. Title and gating should agree.

### Test coverage is thin for the headline use case

The single spec exercises a JS-only entrypoint with a relative import, which doesn't touch the actual motivation (skipping the npm tree). I'd want at least one spec that imports an npm package, runs with `--bundle`, asserts it executes correctly, and ideally asserts the binary is materially smaller than the non-bundled equivalent.

For the known limitations called out in the description (native `.node`, worker entrypoints, dynamic `require(path.join(__dirname,...))`), a couple of specs asserting the current failure mode would lock the limitations into the test matrix rather than leaving them as description-only caveats.

### Smaller observations (non-blocking)

*   Temp bundle is written into `initial_cwd` as `.deno_compile_bundle_<rand>.mjs`. If `deno compile` is killed (SIGKILL) instead of exiting cleanly, the `Drop`\-based guard doesn't run and a `.mjs` file is left in the user's cwd. `std::env::temp_dir()` would be more hygienic, if the bundler doesn't need cwd context to resolve relative paths.
*   `bundle_path.display().to_string()` is lossy on non-UTF-8 paths; pedantic, but `to_string_lossy().into_owned()` is at least explicit about it.
*   The CJS interop fix from [#34533](https://github.com/denoland/deno/pull/34533)
     reaches `--bundle` output via `maybe_process_contents`, so dual CJS/ESM packages should work correctly under `--bundle`. Good.

CI is essentially green.

Thanks for the review. Addressed in [3b6672f](https://github.com/denoland/deno/commit/3b6672f782862d54cc7aabfc8ebe7d364a090212)
:

*   **Cleanup regression**: the framework-entrypoint guard is now constructed up front (`_framework_cleanup`), before the bundle step, so it's removed even if `run_bundle_for_compile` fails and unwinds via `?`. The bundle path is registered for cleanup _before_ it's written too, so a partially-written bundle is also cleaned up.
    
*   **Lossy path**: switched to `to_string_lossy().into_owned()`.
    
*   **temp\_dir**: I kept the bundle in `initial_cwd` rather than `std::env::temp_dir()` after testing both. Writing to the system temp dir bakes the build machine's temp path into the embedded VFS tree (it showed up as `private/tmp/.deno_compile_bundle_*.mjs` plus a `tmp --> private/tmp` symlink), which makes compiled output non-reproducible and platform-dependent. Keeping it next to the project yields a clean relative `main └── .deno_compile_bundle_<hash>.mjs`. Happy to revisit if you'd prefer the temp dir despite that.
    
*   **Test coverage**: added `compile/bundle/npm`, which imports an ESM npm package, runs the binary, and asserts the embedded-files tree contains only the bundled `.mjs` and **no `node_modules`** (proving the npm tree is skipped).
    
*   **CJS**: while writing tests I found CJS npm packages break under `--bundle` — esbuild externalizes them as a runtime `require()` against `node_modules`, which `--bundle` strips. Added `compile/bundle/npm_cjs_unsupported` as an expected-failure spec to lock in the current behavior (to be removed once CJS packages are inlined), and updated the PR description's limitations accordingly.

`[322fa61](https://github.com/denoland/deno/pull/34527/commits/322fa617bd25fa8c63d2ff8b6fea55ef3276f388) `

The two new bundle npm specs hardcoded unix-isms in their expected
output:
- npm/compile.out asserted the embedded-files tree root as \`main\`, but
  the output binary is \`main.exe\` on Windows. Use \`main\[WILDLINE\]\` to
  absorb the suffix (matches the convention in npm\_fs etc.).
- npm\_cjs\_unsupported/run.out asserted the NotCapable path with forward
  slashes, which don't match Windows backslashes. The package name

LGTM for a first cut. The shape is right: reuse the esbuild bundler, write a single `.mjs`, repoint `compile_flags.source_file` at it, and let the existing managed-npm path naturally skip the VFS fill because tree-shaking removes `Module::Npm` entries. Gating the unconditional BYONM `fill_npm_vfs` on `!compile_flags.bundle` is the minimal correct change for that path. Reusing `replace_require_shim` is the right call so dynamic `require()` of `node:` builtins keeps working.

A few substantive points worth addressing — none blocking, but ideally before this graduates from experimental:

1.  **Unstable gating.** This is titled `feat(unstable):` but the only user-visible gate is a `log::warn!`. Other recent experimental compile features sit behind an explicit `--unstable-*` flag or `unstable_features` config check. A warning is easy to miss in CI logs; given the known holes (CJS, native addons, workers, dynamic require), I'd lean toward gating behind `--unstable-compile-bundle` (or `unstable_features`) so users opt in deliberately, and keep the warning as belt-and-suspenders.
    
2.  **Bundle file location.** Writing `.deno_compile_bundle_<rand>.mjs` into `initial_cwd` is justified (avoids baking the build machine's temp path into the binary), but two failure modes worth thinking about:
    
    *   Requires `initial_cwd` to be writable. CI sandboxes, read-only checkouts, and some container setups won't have that.
    *   If the process is killed (SIGKILL, OOM), the `CleanupGuard::drop` never runs and stale `.deno_compile_bundle_*.mjs` files litter the project root. Consider adding the pattern to a suggested `.gitignore` snippet in docs, or recovering stale files at the start of the next compile.
3.  **`--bundle` × `--check` interaction.** All new specs use `--no-check`. What happens if a user passes `--bundle` without `--no-check`? My read is that `compile_binary` ends up running `create_graph_and_maybe_check` on the bundled `.mjs` entrypoint, which is post-transpile JS — so type checking effectively no-ops on the user's original sources. If that's intentional, document it (and add a spec). If not, type-check the original source _before_ swapping in the bundle path.
    
4.  **CJS limitation locked in by `npm_cjs_unsupported`.** The spec asserts the failure mode as a `NotCapable` permission error referencing the host's `node_modules` path — that's brittle (only reproducible on a machine where that path happens to exist and is outside `--allow-read`). On a machine where it doesn't exist, the error wording would change. Consider matching on a more invariant substring (e.g. `cjs-default-export` and `error:`) so the spec isn't sensitive to host file layout.
    
5.  **`bundle.rs` minor.** `bundle_for_compile` returns the first JS output it sees and bails if none — fine for `code_splitting: false`, just worth a comment that this single-output assumption is intentional and would need to change if splitting is ever enabled here.
    

Approving so this can land and iterate. Keep the experimental warning prominent in the changelog when 2.x ships this.

First cut at making \`deno compile\` ship a bundled entrypoint instead of
embedding the entire \`node\_modules/\` tree verbatim. Motivated by a
real-world report comparing \`deno compile\` against \`bun build --compile\`
on a 2700-module CLI, where Deno's binary was ~3x bigger almost entirely
because of the raw npm payload. The flag is gated behind a "this is
experimental" warning since several real cases aren't handled yet.

When \`--bundle\` is set, the entrypoint is run through the existing
esbuild-based bundler (ESM, platform=Deno, packages=Bundle,
tree-shaking on) and the bundle is written to a temp \`.mjs\` next to the
source. The standalone binary writer then sees a single self-contained
file in the graph, so the existing managed-npm path naturally skips the
VFS fill (no \`Module::Npm\` entries left after tree-shaking). The BYONM
path, which fills the VFS unconditionally, is gated on the new flag.
The existing \`replace\_require\_shim\` rewrite is reused so esbuild's
"Dynamic require not supported" stub becomes a real
\`createRequire(import.meta.url)\` call against \`node:module\`, so dynamic
\`require()\` of \`node:\` builtins keeps working in denort.

Known limitations for this PR (intentional, to keep it reviewable):
native \`.node\` addons, worker entrypoints, and any module that does
dynamic \`require(path.join(\_\_dirname, ...))\` aren't traced and will
break. CJS npm packages are also currently externalized by esbuild as a
runtime \`require()\` against \`node\_modules\`, which \`--bundle\` strips, so
those break too; this is locked in by an expected-failure spec
(\`compile/bundle/npm\_cjs\_unsupported\`) that should be removed once CJS
packages are inlined into the bundle. The warning calls out the
experimental status.
